papers.source_abstract: ABSTRACT Achieving human‐skin‐like multidimensional tactile perception in self‐powered electronics remains fundamentally constrained by the intrinsic trade‐offs among sensitivity, mechanical compliance, and electrical output. To overcome these bottlenecks, a biomimetic “mille‐feuille” triboelectric sensor is engineered via hierarchical nanofibrous membranes, transitioning conventional 2D interfacial contact into 3D volumetric nesting to significantly increase the effective contact area. Incorporating a zwitterionic polymer poly(sulfobetaine methacrylate) (PSBMA) into the triboelectric matrix enables multiscale enhancement of dielectric polarization, charge trapping, interfacial contact, and mechanical robustness. This integrated design concurrently improves surface charge density and contact area, culminating in a remarkable 2.16‐fold enhancement in triboelectric performance compared to pristine counterparts. The sensor exhibits an ultra‐low detection limit (1.21 Pa), a broad working range (2.45–100 kPa), fast response and recovery times (35 and 29 ms), and excellent durability over 10 000 cycles. Beyond conventional motion monitoring, integrating this sensor with a robotic gripper and a convolutional neural network (CNN) enables active material cognition. The system demonstrated accurate recognition and sorting of geometrically identical objects, reaching 100% test accuracy under current dataset and sorting of geometrically identical objects based on their material‐dependent tactile responses during physical interaction. This work provides a robust material‐algorithm synergistic paradigm for intelligent robotics and tactile sensing applications.

papers.source_abstract: ABSTRACT Gallium‐based liquid metals (LMs), due to their extremely high surface tension, are incompatible with conventional manufacturing processes, thereby hindering high‐precision patterning and becoming a serious bottleneck for their application in flexible electronic devices. Here, we present a facile shear‐oxidation modulation strategy and introduce a mass‐evolution‐derived effective oxide‐state descriptor (Φ ox ) for quantitatively evaluating shear‐conditioned liquid‐metal systems. Under ambient shear, the native gallium oxide skin is continuously ruptured and incorporated into the liquid metal matrix, forming an oxide‐enriched metastable microstructure. This structure enhances flow resistance, induces pronounced shear‐thinning behavior, and produces a yield‐like threshold, thereby suppressing surface‐tension‐driven relaxation. Guided by Φ ox ‐based state selection, we demonstrate that a representative low‐Φ ox state enables stable direct writing of low‐interference interconnects, whereas a representative high‐Φ ox state supports blade coating combined with laser patterning for fabricating high‐fidelity features and robust strain‐sensing units. Further integration of these state‐partitioned LM states into interference‐resistant wearable gloves yields reliable multi‐channel motion signals, enabling 100% gesture‐recognition accuracy with a lightweight Transformer model and supporting real‐time robotic‐hand control. These findings highlight oxide‐state engineering as a route to balance fluidity, pattern stability, and electrical functionality in Ga‐based LMs, providing a foundation for scalable flexible electronics and human‐machine interfaces.

papers.source_abstract: ABSTRACT Chitosan, a polysaccharide upcycled from biowaste, has long promised sustainable, biocompatible, and antimicrobial films and devices, an appeal reinforced by its recent regulatory recognition, with several chitosan‐based antibacterial dressings gaining clearance through the Food and Drug Administration's 510(k) pathway. Yet despite this momentum, its role in electronics has remained confined to single‐device demonstrations. Here, we introduce a multilayer electronic platform built entirely on chitosan films, shifting its role from a mere material component to a system‐level enabler. Using a low‐cost, ambient‐temperature, chemical‐free cutter‐based method, we directly pattern copper traces on flexible chitosan films at ∼750 µm resolution and stack them into soft multilayer circuits; an optional microfabrication step is employed solely for chips with sub‐100 µm pad pitch. We mount off‐the‐shelf microelectronics—including amplifiers, light‐emitting diodes (LEDs), photodetectors, integrated circuits (ICs), resistors, and capacitors—directly onto the patterned chitosan circuits, assembling complete functional systems such as wireless near field communication (NFC) and Ultra High Frequency (UHF) Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) tags and fully operational Photoplethysmography (PPG) sensors, all seamlessly integrated within the chitosan platform. Notably, the UHF tag with an embedded temperature sensor demonstrates readings with better than 1°C accuracy, enabling practical applications in wearable monitoring, such as wound healing, as well as in food safety tracking. Beyond electronics, we uncover a crucial biological edge. Using a Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) expressing E. coli strain, a transient loss of fluorescence and growth was observed during chitosan exposure, followed by full recovery upon film removal, with bacterial viability, plasmid stability, and normal metabolic function fully preserved. This unique, reversible, and controllable bacteriostatic effect underscores chitosan's potential as a safe, biocompatible substrate that, when integrated with electronics, enables the development of next‐generation wearable, implantable, and environmental monitoring devices.

papers.source_abstract: ABSTRACT Flexible perovskite solar cells (f‐PSCs) hold immense promise for next‐generation wearable and portable photovoltaic applications, yet their commercialization is severely impeded by interfacial non‐radiative recombination and insufficient mechanical durability at the SnO 2 /perovskite interface. Here, we demonstrate a dual‐modulation molecular bridge strategy using the plant‐derived amino acid derivative potassium acetyl‐L‐lysinate (P‐AcL), deposited as an ultrathin interlayer on pre‐annealed SnO 2 films, to simultaneously address both challenges. P‐AcL forms robust bidentate carboxyl coordination and amino hydrogen‐bonding with SnO 2 films, passivating surface oxygen vacancies, optimizing interfacial energy alignment, and inhibiting buried‐interface thermal decomposition. Its long alkyl chain and amide groups extend toward the perovskite layer, dual‐anchoring undercoordinated Pb 2+ and iodide vacancy defects, releasing residual thermal stress, guiding high‐quality perovskite crystallization, and mitigating bending‐induced interfacial delamination. Benefiting from this synergy, air‐processed f‐PSCs (20% RH) achieve a champion power conversion efficiency of 25.21%, and retain >24% PCE even under 40% RH. The modified devices retain 85.6% and 90.2% of their initial PCE after 10 000 convex and concave bending cycles at a 5 mm radius, respectively, alongside improved light and thermal stability. This work provides a simple, green, scalable route toward high‐efficiency, stable flexible perovskite photovoltaics.

papers.source_abstract: ABSTRACT The development of flexible wearable films integrating high electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding effectiveness (SE), multimodal thermal management, and adaptability to complex environments remains a major challenge. Herein, a multifunctional asymmetric ultrathin film composed of a silver nanowires (AgNWs)/waterborne polyurethane (WPU) layer, FeCoNi/polyacrylonitrile‌ fibrous layer, and FeCo@Ti 3 C 2 T x /WPU layer was successfully fabricated through electrospinning combined with a layered blade‐coating strategy. The AgNWs network and FeCo@Ti 3 C 2 T x magnetoelectric coupling yielded an average EMI SE of 78.17 dB, with absorption as the primary shielding mechanism (SE A /SE T = 93.61%). Furthermore, stable dual‐mode electrothermal/photothermal was achieved by exploiting the high conductivity of AgNWs and the excellent photothermal conversion capability of FeCo@Ti 3 C 2 T x . Saturated temperatures of 120.1°C and 76.4°C were reached under a voltage of 1.0 V and light irradiation of 300 mW cm −2 , respectively, accompanied by rapid thermal response and excellent cycling stability. Notably, typical Janus wettability characteristics were also observed, with water contact angles of 70.27° and 122.22° on the two sides. The film demonstrates significant integrated advantages in electromagnetic protection, intelligent thermal management, and complex‐environment adaptability, providing a feasible pathway for the practical development of next‐generation intelligent flexible wearable electronics.

papers.source_abstract: ABSTRACT Chemical reactions offer a powerful strategy for generating visible optical responses through localized changes in absorption, dielectric environment, and interfacial wetting. A palladium (Pd)‐embedded Fabry–Perot cavity is introduced as a reaction‐active optical platform in which structural color is governed by intracavity absorption coupled with reaction‐induced dielectric perturbation. Positioning Pd within the dielectric spacer creates a spatially controllable reactive absorber whose vertical location relative to the standing‐wave field dictates wavelength‐selective absorption within the cavity. The morphology of the embedded Pd layer provides an additional design parameter by modulating both optical loss and interfacial wetting. Under hydrogen exposure in the presence of oxygen, catalytic water formation at the Pd/polymer interface generates localized dielectric heterogeneity and interfacial water droplets, thereby perturbing the optical path length and amplifying the visible response. As a result, the cavity exhibits pronounced, morphology‐dependent color transitions that are inaccessible through dielectric‐layer engineering or Pd/PdH refractive‐index changes alone, enabling direct visual hydrogen sensing under ambient light, as well as flexible optical devices capable of large‐area patterning. These findings establish a design framework for reaction‐active optical cavities that translate localized chemistry into a colorimetric hydrogen sensing mechanism.
